You did not understand and ask for the sentence to be repeated slowly.
Good morning. Do you speak English?
A polite morning greeting plus a safe check that the other person speaks English.
Good morning. Do you speak English?
At a morning information desk, a polite selamat pagi opens the conversation.

Good morning. Indonesian greetings are time-specific: selamat pagi (morning), selamat siang (mid-day), selamat sore (late afternoon), selamat malam (evening). The time-of-day greeting feels more natural than a flat halo in a polite service exchange.
Bright morning at the information desk, a polite first question in Indonesian.

On the sidewalk, politely ask where the station is.

A polite repair phrase when the conversation moved too fast.

The conversation pauses briefly while you ask for a slow repeat with pelan-pelan.

Not (for verbs and adjectives). Use tidak to negate verbs and adjectives — tidak mengerti (don't understand), tidak panas (not hot). For nouns and identity, switch to bukan instead: Saya bukan turis (I am not a tourist).
A short pause in the conversation, a friendly request to slow down.
On the sidewalk, politely ask where the station is.
At a cafe counter, order one coffee politely.
Excuse me, where is the station?
A short polite where-question with a quick apology to open.
Excuse me, where is the station?
On the sidewalk, you ask a short, polite question: where is the station?

Where. The standard where-question in Indonesian. Notice there is no separate verb for "is" — Indonesian skips the copula at A1, so Di mana stasiun? is literally "Where station?". The textbook spelling is two words; you will often see dimana typed together informally.
A sunny street corner, a visible station sign, a short question for directions.
At a cafe counter, order one coffee politely.
In a small shop, ask the price of the item in front of you.
A very practical order — no verb conjugation, no articles.
At the cafe, the order stays short: one coffee, tolong.

Coffee. Indonesia is one of the world's biggest coffee producers, and kopi shares the same root as English coffee (both ultimately from Arabic qahwa). Indonesian has no articles, so kopi covers "a coffee", "the coffee", or just "coffee" depending on context.
A bright cafe counter, a cup of coffee, a short polite order.
In a small shop, ask the price of the item in front of you.
At the station, ask what time the train arrives.
The short standard question for asking a price in a shop.
In a small shop, you point at an item and ask: berapa harganya?

How much / how many. Berapa covers both — Indonesian does not split countable from uncountable the way English does. The -nya ending on harganya is a small A1 helper meaning "of it / its", so the question feels native without a separate pronoun.
A small shop, a price tag, a short question about harganya.
At the station, ask what time the train arrives.
At a pharmacy or help desk, ask a male attendant for help politely.
What time does the train arrive?
A clear time question at the station.
What time does the train arrive?
At the station, the timetable is in front of you and you ask what time the train arrives.

Hour / o'clock. Jam is the A1 anchor for clock time. Jam berapa asks the time without changing any verb form, because Indonesian signals tense with time words (besok = tomorrow, kemarin = yesterday) rather than conjugation. Heads-up: in Indonesian kereta means "train" — in Malay the same word means "car", a common trap if you have studied either language before.
A station with a clock and arrivals board, a clear question about the time.
At a pharmacy or help desk, ask a male attendant for help politely.
Inside a cafe or shop, make a short positive comment about the place.
A direct, polite request for help in a service moment.
At the help desk, you greet a Pak and ask for help with tolong.

Please (request marker). Tolong sits at the start of a request, right before the verb: tolong bantu, tolong ulangi. It is more practical at A1 than the more formal mohon. Use silakan instead when you are inviting someone to do something ("please come in", "please go ahead").
A service desk, a respectful Pak greeting, a direct request for help.
Inside a cafe or shop, make a short positive comment about the place.
Confirm a simple plan for tomorrow at seven.
A short positive small-talk line about the place.
In a bright cafe, you offer a quick positive comment: di sini bagus.

Here. Di sini is the standard form for "here". Notice there is no "is" between "here" and "nice" — Indonesian skips the copula at A1, so Di sini bagus is literally "Here nice". The textbook spelling is two words; you will often see disini typed together informally.
A bright cafe, a short positive comment about the place.
Confirm a simple plan for tomorrow at seven.
Close the interaction with thanks and a neutral goodbye.
A short confirmation of a plan for the next day.
A small plan lands clearly: tomorrow at seven, good.

Tomorrow. Besok puts a sentence in the future without any verb change — Indonesian uses time words instead of tense conjugation. Pair it with kemarin (yesterday) and sekarang (now) and you can talk about all three time frames at A1.
A small calendar, the time set to seven, a friendly confirmation.
Close the interaction with thanks and a neutral goodbye.
You have completed Indonesian A1 Practical 1.
A clear thank-you plus a neutral goodbye.
After being helped, you close with terima kasih and sampai jumpa.

Thank you. Terima kasih is the standard form. The textbook spelling is two words; you will often see terimakasih typed together informally. The reply is usually sama-sama (mutual, literally "same-same") or kembali (back) — both mean "you're welcome" at A1.
A counter farewell, a short thank-you, a neutral goodbye.

At a small counter, admit that you are confused and ask for simple help.
At a desk, ask a staff member to write down exact information.
Sorry, I'm confused. Can you help me?
A natural A1 line when you need simple help, not just a repeat.
Sorry, I'm confused. Can you help me?
In a small shop, you say "maaf, saya bingung," then ask for simple help.
The standard word for the mental state. Indonesian uses bare adjectives without any "to be" — "Saya bingung" works as a complete sentence with no copula.
A counter exchange where the learner pauses and asks for help.

At a desk, ask a staff member to write down exact information.
With a phone map open, ask someone to show the place on the map.
Please write this name down, ma'am.
A polite, direct request to capture something precisely in writing.
Please write this name down, ma'am.
At the service desk, you ask "Bu" to write the name so the information is exact.
Plain base form for 'write' — Indonesian doesn't conjugate verbs for person. 'Tulis' is the same form whether saya, Anda, or dia is doing the writing.
A service desk with a pen and paper for exact information.

With a phone map open, ask someone to show the place on the map.
At a bakery counter, ask between two visible options.
Can you show me on the map?
A short request when a map or phone is visible.
Can you show me on the map?
You open the map on your phone and ask the person to point out the place.
Standard word for both paper and digital maps. Heads up: "bisa" in this lesson means "can / be able to" — in other contexts it can also mean "venom"; context separates them.
A phone map on a counter, with a finger pointing at a place.

At a bakery counter, ask between two visible options.
In a small shop, ask whether the item is available now.
The natural short question when two things are visible.
At a bakery, you point at two options and ask: this one or that one?
Pairs with "ini" (this) for the near/far split. Indonesian has no articles — "yang ini" and "yang itu" carry the demonstrative role on their own.
Two pastries in a case, one near and one farther away.
Small help and simple choices in Indonesian
In a small shop, ask whether the item is available now.
At the till, ask whether card payment is possible.
A clear service question about current availability.
In a small shop, you point at an item and ask if it's available.
Standard A1 Indonesian — not an English mix. Indonesian has no copula: 'ini tersedia' literally reads 'this available' with no 'is'. 'Apakah' at the front turns it into a yes/no question.
A small shop shelf, one item under discussion.
Small help and simple choices in Indonesian
At the till, ask whether card payment is possible.
At the end of a purchase, ask for a receipt and a bag.
A short, natural question at the end of a purchase.
At the till, you hold up your card and ask if card payment works.
Standard word for any payment or plastic card. 'Dengan kartu' (with card) follows the verb to mark the means: 'bayar dengan kartu' = 'pay by card'.
A card held at the cashier counter.
Small help and simple choices in Indonesian
At the end of a purchase, ask for a receipt and a bag.
At a restaurant host stand, say that you have a reservation.
May I have a receipt and a bag, please?
A polite closing request for the receipt and a bag.
May I have a receipt and a bag, please?
At the end of shopping, you calmly ask for a receipt and a bag.
Very common shopping word. Indonesian doesn't mark plurals — 'tas' can mean 'bag' or 'bags' from context, with reduplication ('tas-tas') used for emphasis.
A checkout counter with a receipt and a shopping bag.

At a restaurant host stand, say that you have a reservation.
Before committing to an item or vehicle, confirm that it is the correct one.
I have a reservation under Meyer.
A clear service line at the host stand, with no hotel-specific room vocabulary.
I have a reservation under Meyer.
In front of the restaurant, you tell the host you have a reservation under Meyer.
Naturalized Indonesian service word — not English code-switching. Standard in restaurants and hotels. The frame "saya punya X" (I have X) works for any A1 possession.
A restaurant host stand with a reservation list.

At a counter, ask for a brief moment while you find a card.
A short safety check before buying, boarding, or choosing.
Before choosing, you ask whether this is the right one.
All-purpose confirmation word. Works for 'is this the right one?', 'did I hear that right?' and similar A1 checks — no travel-specific noun like 'kereta' or 'kamar' required.
A learner checks an item before committing.
Small help and simple choices in Indonesian
At a counter, ask for a brief moment while you find a card.
One moment, I'm looking for my card.
A natural short pause without a long explanation.
One moment, I'm looking for my card.
At the till, you say "sebentar" while searching for your card.
Standard short-wait expression. Polite enough in any service context — no need to escalate to the more formal 'mohon'.
A checkout pause while looking for a card.
Directions, buses, and simple travel choices in Indonesian
On the sidewalk, ask politely whether to turn left or right.
Mid-navigation, ask whether the place is still far on foot.
A short, safe direction question when you reach an intersection.
At the intersection, you pause briefly and ask: left or right?
Standard A1 word for left. Always pairs with kanan (right) — together they anchor every Indonesian direction-giving exchange. The preposition ke (to / toward) marks the direction.
A sidewalk intersection with left and right direction signs.

Mid-navigation, ask whether the place is still far on foot.
In front of a shop, ask politely whether it is still open now.
Is it still far on foot?
A practical distance check before you keep walking.
Is it still far on foot?
On the sidewalk, you ask whether the place is still far on foot.
Simple A1 distance word, pairs with dekat (near). No case marking, no gender, no agreement — Indonesian adjectives stay the same in every position.
A sunny sidewalk with a destination sign down the street.

In front of a shop, ask politely whether it is still open now.
At a bus stop, ask which bus goes to the museum.
A short check at the door so you don't walk in for nothing.
In front of the shop, you look at the door and ask whether it is still open now.
Everyday word for both "open" (state) and "to open" (action) — Indonesian doesn't split them. Its opposite tutup (closed) shows up here for contrast.
A shop door with an open sign and daylight outside.
Directions, buses, and simple travel choices in Indonesian
At a bus stop, ask which bus goes to the museum.
On a moving bus, confirm whether the next stop is the museum.
Excuse me, which bus goes to the museum?
A clear route question — not just asking where a bus is parked.
Excuse me, which bus goes to the museum?
At the stop, you see several buses and ask which bus goes to the museum.
Naturalized loanword — same spelling as English. The connector yang (the one that / which) is how Indonesian builds relative clauses: "bus yang ke museum" = "the bus that [goes] to the museum."
A bus stop with several route numbers and a museum icon.

On a moving bus, confirm whether the next stop is the museum.
At a transit counter, ask for one ticket to the city.
Is the next stop the museum?
A quick safety check before you get off.
Is the next stop the museum?
Inside the bus, you get ready to get off and confirm the next stop.
Naturalized Indonesian transit word for bus or tram stops — borrowed from Dutch "halte." The suffix -nya in berikutnya means "the" — literally "the following one."
Inside a bus near the doors, the next-stop display visible.

Outside a shop or museum, ask what time it closes today.

One ticket to the city, please.
At the small ticket window, you ask for one ticket to the city with "tolong."
Naturalized English loanword — instantly recognizable to English-L1 learners. "Karcis" also exists for transit and admission tickets, but "tiket" is the safer A1 default.
A ticket counter with one small transit ticket.

Outside a shop or museum, ask what time it closes today.
At an intersection, ask whether the place is on the street corner.

A planning question before you start your visit.
What time does it close today?
In front of the museum, you ask what time it closes today.
Standard counterpart to buka (open). The form stays the same for opening hours, the past, the future — Indonesian doesn't conjugate verbs for person or tense.
A museum entrance with an opening-hours board.

At an intersection, ask whether the place is on the street corner.
At the end of a long walk, choose between walking and taking a taxi.
Is the place on the street corner?
A precise landmark question at the intersection.
Is the place on the street corner?
At the intersection, you look for the place on the street corner.
Standard word for corner or angle. "Sudut jalan" (street corner) is a clear landmark image — note Indonesian builds compound landmarks by noun + noun, no preposition between them.
A street corner with a small shop on it.
Directions, buses, and simple travel choices in Indonesian
At the end of a long walk, choose between walking and taking a taxi.
On transit, say you got off at the wrong stop and ask for help.
Should we walk or take a taxi?
A neutral shared decision without any formal address.
Should we walk or take a taxi?
After walking, we choose: on foot or by taxi.
Standardized Indonesian spelling. "Naik" is the all-purpose verb for boarding any vehicle (taxi, bus, train, plane) — much wider than English "take" or "board."
A sidewalk at dusk with a taxi waiting nearby.

On transit, say you got off at the wrong stop and ask for help.
Sorry, I got off at the wrong stop. Can you help me?
A calm recovery phrase after a small transit mistake.
I got off at the wrong stop.
Sorry, I got off at the wrong stop. Can you help me?
At the wrong stop, you stay calm and ask for help.
Simple word for getting off transit or going down. "Salah turun" (wrong + get-off) keeps the apology short and natural — Indonesian builds many error phrases with salah + verb.
A transit stop after getting off too early or too late.
Restaurants, drinks, and short conversations in Indonesian
At a restaurant entrance, ask for a table for two.
Seated at a table, ask to see the menu.
A short service request at the host stand — no pronouns or extra politeness needed.
At the restaurant entrance, the request stays short: a table for two.
Standard A1 word for table. In restaurants it works directly with "untuk" plus a number — no articles, no plural marking on "orang" (person/people).

Seated at a table, ask to see the menu.
At a cafe table, order hot tea politely.
A polite, short request before ordering.
At the restaurant table, you ask to see the menu before ordering.
Naturalized Indonesian restaurant word — same spelling as English, but standard local usage, not code-switching. "Boleh" + verb is the polite "may I..." frame.

At a cafe table, order hot tea politely.
At a cafe counter, specify that you do not want sugar.
A simple drink order with 'saya mau' — no articles, no verb conjugation needed.
At the cafe, you order hot tea with a short sentence.
Standard word for tea — pairs naturally with the earlier kopi order. Note the order: noun then adjective (teh panas = tea hot), opposite of English.
A cafe table with a cup of hot tea.

At a cafe counter, specify that you do not want sugar.
At a bakery or counter, ask whether the bread is still fresh.
At the cafe, you keep the order simple: without sugar.
Standard A1 word for sugar. 'Tanpa' (without) is the preposition for absence — shorter and more natural than building a long 'don't want sugar' sentence with 'tidak'.
A cafe counter with sugar packets beside a cup.

At a cafe counter, add one bread roll or piece of bread to your order.
A polite quality check at the counter.
At the bakery, you point at the bread and ask whether it is still fresh.
Standard word for fresh — works for food, drinks, or air. No gender or number changes; Indonesian adjectives keep one form for everything.
A bakery counter with fresh bread on display.

At a cafe counter, add one bread roll or piece of bread to your order.
At a cafe counter, ask for the order to be takeaway.
Yes, one bread roll too, please.
A short yes when staff asks if you want anything else.
Yes, one bread roll too, please.
Asked if there's anything else, you say yes and add one bread.
Common A1 food word — covers bread and simple baked goods. No plural marking: "satu roti" = "one bread," "dua roti" = "two breads/rolls."
A cafe counter with one bread roll added to the order.

After eating or drinking, give a brief positive verdict.
A short takeaway phrase for food or drink.
At the cafe till, you ask for the order to be taken away.
Means "home" or "back home." In "dibawa pulang" (passive: to be taken home) it forms the natural Indonesian way to say "takeaway."

A short, warm compliment after eating or drinking.
After eating, you give a brief compliment: this is delicious.
The everyday A1 compliment for food and drink — short, warm, used constantly. Can also describe comfort more broadly ("tidur enak" = sleep well, "badan enak" = feel good).
A finished plate and a simple pleased expression.

At the end of a meal, ask for the bill politely.
A neutral, light small-talk line at the counter.
In the cafe queue, you make a light comment: it's busy today.
Describes a busy place or day — standard Bahasa Indonesia, not a Jakarta colloquialism. Different from "sibuk" (busy meaning occupied with tasks).

At the end of a meal, ask for the bill politely.
May I have the bill, please?
A polite closing request at the restaurant table.
May I have the bill, please?
At the end of the meal, you politely ask for the bill.
Standard A1 word — avoids the English code-mix "bill." "Bon" exists for small slips/receipts but "tagihan" is the right word for a restaurant bill.

You arrive late and apologize simply.
You realize you forgot something and apologize.
A short, clear apology with no long explanation.
When you arrive late, just say: sorry, I'm late.
Standard word for late. Indonesian uses it as a bare adjective with no copula: "Saya terlambat" literally reads "I late."
Arriving a little late to a simple appointment.

You realize you forgot something and apologize.
In first contact, ask the other person’s name politely.
Name a small slip honestly and briefly.
For a small slip, "saya lupa" is already clear enough.
Very common A1 word — covers both "forget" and "forgot." Indonesian doesn't mark past tense on the verb; context (or a time word like kemarin) does the work.
A small forgotten-item moment at a counter.

In first contact, ask the other person’s name politely.
After introductions, say that it is nice to meet the person.
A safe name question for a new conversation.
When meeting someone new, the "nama Anda" question stays polite and clear.
Standard A1 word. Note: Indonesian literally asks "Who is your name?" — "siapa" (who) is the question word for names, not "apa" (what). Pairing with Anda keeps it polite anywhere in the archipelago.

After introductions, say that it is nice to meet the person.
In a light first conversation, ask where the person is from.
A warm, polite reply after exchanging names.
After exchanging names, you reply with "senang bertemu."
Standard form for meet. The ber- prefix marks a verb that doesn't take a direct object — "meet WITH" needs the preposition "dengan," never just "bertemu Anda."
Two people meeting politely after exchanging names.

A polite origin question with no slang shortcut.

Standard Bahasa Indonesia — more formal than the casual shortcut "dari mana?" Fits polite first-meeting register at A1.

In polite social planning, ask whether the person has time tonight.
A simple where-do-you-live question in polite register.
In a new neighborhood, you ask whether the person lives here.
Means "live" or "stay" (also "be left behind" — context distinguishes). The verb form is identical for saya, Anda, dia — no person conjugation.
A quiet street conversation near an apartment entrance.

In polite social planning, ask whether the person has time tonight.
Suggest the cafe as a simple meeting place.
A careful availability check for the evening.
For social plans, "malam ini" gives a clear time slot.
Covers both evening and night — English splits these but Indonesian doesn't. "Malam ini" (this evening / tonight) puts the time on the adverb; no verb tense needed.
Evening street light outside a small cafe.

A short, neutral suggestion for a meeting place.
Shall we meet at the cafe?
For a casual plan, "kita bertemu di kafe" sounds light and easy.
Standardized Indonesian spelling. The French "café" is tolerated as a typing variant. Note "kita" — the inclusive "we" that includes the listener; "kami" excludes them.

Suggest maybe tomorrow when today does not work.
Close the conversation with a see-you-tomorrow goodbye.
A short, soft postponement without a hard no.
When today doesn't work, "mungkin besok" keeps the plan light.
Standard marker for maybe. Time comes from "besok" (tomorrow), not from any verb form — Indonesian leaves verbs untouched and lets adverbs carry tense.
A small planning pause with tomorrow marked on a calendar.
Apologies, meeting people, and simple plans in Indonesian
Close the conversation with a see-you-tomorrow goodbye.
A friendly close when the next meeting is already set.
At the end of the conversation, "sampai jumpa besok" closes the plan warmly.
Standard everyday goodbye. "Selamat tinggal" (formal farewell) feels more final — used when leaving someone behind for a long time, not for a casual see-you-tomorrow.
A friendly goodbye at the end of a simple plan.

When feeling unwell, 'saya sakit' and 'tolong bantu saya' are clear enough.
Core word covering both "sick" (state) and "hurting" (pain). The form stays the same after saya, Anda, or dia — no agreement.

On the sidewalk, "apakah ada apotek dekat sini" asks calmly for directions.

At a pharmacy counter, ask for medicine in a general A1 way.
Point to a body location and say it hurts without diagnosing it.
A general request at the counter, with no specific condition.

A concrete pain statement using a body word plus pointing.
While pointing, "kaki saya sakit di sini" gives the location without naming an illness.
Indonesian "kaki" covers both foot and leg — English splits them. Possession comes from word order: "kaki saya" (literally "foot I") = "my foot" — no possessive form needed.

In a pharmacy, cafe, or social setting, ask politely for water.

Head. Indonesian builds symptoms with sakit + body part: sakit kepala (headache), sakit perut (stomachache), sakit gigi (toothache) — predictable A1 pattern.

A help-and-location question, not an emergency call.

Naturalized loanword from Dutch "dokter." One form covers male and female — Indonesian has no grammatical gender, so the noun never changes.

At a pharmacy, restaurant, or hotel, disclose an allergy in plain terms.
In public, ask another person to call for help without escalating to an emergency claim.
A clear A1 allergy disclosure without medical details.
At a restaurant or pharmacy, "saya alergi kacang" gives important information briefly.
Standardized Indonesian form. Works as both noun and adjective — "saya alergi kacang" literally reads "I allergic nut(s)." No gender or number agreement needed.
Restaurant or pharmacy allergy disclosure with a nut icon.

In public, ask another person to call for help without escalating to an emergency claim.
At the end of a pharmacy or first-aid moment, say you feel better and thank the helper.
A short request for help — deliberately not an emergency call or alarm.
